clinical_category: Spinal motion restriction - safer transfer technique
blueprint_topic: Prevention of secondary movement during transfer of a client with suspected unstable spinal injury
stem: A trauma client with a suspected unstable spinal injury must be transferred from one flat surface to another while spinal motion restriction is maintained. Which approach is best supported by current evidence?

options.A: Use a coordinated lift-and-slide transfer with manual spinal stabilization when feasible
options.B: Use a log-roll for every transfer because it consistently produces the least spinal motion
options.C: Have the client twist the shoulders and pelvis separately to help the team complete the transfer
options.D: Allow an unassisted side roll because manual stabilization is unnecessary during transfer

rationale: A is correct. The 2024 Wilderness Medical Society clinical practice guideline recommends lift-and-slide transfer rather than log-roll when spinal motion restriction is desired, based on biomechanical evidence showing better stabilization with lift-and-slide techniques. A 2026 systematic review likewise found that log-roll consistently generated greater angular or translational displacement than several alternative transfer methods in unstable-spine models, although direct clinical evidence of neurologic worsening remains limited. Therefore the safest answer is a coordinated low-motion transfer with manual stabilization when feasible. B overstates the log-roll as universally superior. C and D deliberately introduce uncontrolled spinal motion.
educational_objective: When transferring a client with a suspected unstable spinal injury, use a coordinated low-motion technique with manual stabilization; do not assume that routine log-rolling is always the lowest-motion transfer method.
source_organization: Wilderness Medical Society (WMS), corroborated by peer-reviewed systematic review evidence
source_document_title: Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for Spinal Cord Protection: 2024 Update; Is the log-roll still safe? A systematic review of patient transfer techniques in traumatic spinal cord injury
source_version_date: WMS guideline published 2024; systematic review published 2026; current evidence checked 2026-08-18
source_locator: WMS 2024 guideline → section 'Moving the Patient with Real or Potential Spine Injury': lift-and-slide transfer provides superior stabilization compared with log-roll; recommendation prefers lift-and-slide with manual stabilization when motion restriction is desired. 2026 systematic review → Results/Conclusions: across unstable-spine models, log-roll generated greater angular/translational displacement than several alternative transfer techniques; direct clinical-outcome evidence remains limited.
source_claim_supported: Current guideline and systematic-review evidence support coordinated lift-and-slide transfer as a lower-motion option than routine log-roll when spinal motion restriction is desired, while avoiding the unsupported claim that log-roll is always unsafe or always causes neurologic injury.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control client-needs subcategory (10–16% of items); this item tests prevention of secondary injury during movement and transfer of a client with suspected spinal instability.
correction_summary: Total clinical rebuild. The original item treated log-roll as the universally safest transfer technique. Current evidence no longer supports that simplification. The final item tests the current preference for a coordinated lift-and-slide low-motion transfer when feasible and does not claim that log-roll is never appropriate in other clinical circumstances.
audit_findings: The original generic AANN source and universal log-roll claim were not adequate under current evidence.
The 2024 WMS guideline specifically prefers lift-and-slide over log-roll when motion restriction is desired.
A 2026 systematic review independently corroborates greater measured spinal displacement with log-roll than with several alternative transfer techniques in unstable-spine models.
The final item preserves uncertainty by not claiming proven neurologic harm from log-roll or that log-roll is never clinically appropriate.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely best answer, no second defensible option within the stated transfer scenario, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
